report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is *plausible but not established*. There is one notable randomized study of acupuncture as an **add-on** for antenatal depression, but it was explicitly a feasibility trial—not definitive evidence that acupuncture itself reduces clinically important depression symptoms.

That 2020 pragmatic RCT compared individualized acupuncture with progressive-muscle relaxation plus usual hospital care; it is described as a feasibility study in the *Journal of Affective Disorders*. Its design means any apparent benefit could partly reflect added attention, expectations, or relaxation rather than needling-specific effects. It also does not show that acupuncture can replace psychotherapy, medication when indicated, or routine perinatal mental-health care.  
https://bmas.blog/2020/07/21/acupuncture-for-antenatal-depression/

Systematic-review evidence for acupuncture in depression generally finds possible symptom benefit, but applicability to pregnancy is weak: studies vary substantially, many lack credible sham controls, and evidence quality is limited.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31370200/  
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/nur.22284

Major perinatal-care guidance instead addresses depression using assessment, psychological therapies, and (when benefits outweigh risks) medication; acupuncture is not a standard recommended treatment for antenatal depression.  
https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg192/chapter/Recommendations

**Practical takeaway:** Someone who enjoys acupuncture might consider it only as a complementary option, discussed with their obstetric and mental-health clinicians, rather than relying on it alone. Depression in pregnancy deserves prompt assessment—especially with worsening symptoms, impaired functioning, or any thoughts of self-harm.
